pages.x: Iraq and Iran had long quarrelled over the Shatt al-Arab, the river where the Tigris and Euphrates flow into the Gulf. In 1979 the revolution in Iran threw its army into chaos, and Ayatollah Khomeini called on the Shia Muslims of Iraq, a majority there, to rise against their rulers. In Baghdad, Saddam Hussein saw a threat, and a chance.

On 22 September 1980 Iraqi planes struck Iranian airfields and Iraqi tanks rolled into Khuzestan, Iran's oil province, where many people speak Arabic. Saddam expected a war of weeks. After a month of street fighting his troops took the port of Khorramshahr, which Iranians renamed Khuninshahr, the city of blood.

Iran answered with huge numbers of volunteers, many of them barely trained teenagers of the Basij militia, who charged across minefields and into machine-gun fire. In May 1982 Iran took back Khorramshahr and soon drove the Iraqis out. Khomeini then decided to carry the war into Iraq, and it went on for six more years.

The front sank into trenches, barbed wire and mud, like the Western Front in the First World War. Iraq used poison gas again and again against Iranian troops. In the war of the cities the two sides fired missiles at each other's capitals, and families in Tehran and Baghdad slept in shelters.

Both sides attacked oil tankers in the Gulf, and the US Navy began escorting ships through it. In July 1988 an American warship, mistaking an Iranian airliner for an attacking jet, shot it down, killing all 290 people aboard.

In March 1988 Iranian troops and Kurdish fighters took Halabja, a Kurdish town inside Iraq. The next day Iraqi planes dropped poison gas on it, and families died in their homes and in the streets as they ran. It was part of the Anfal, a campaign in which Saddam's forces killed tens of thousands of Iraq's Kurds.
pages.of: people killed by gas in one day

pages.x: In July 1988, with his armies worn out, Khomeini accepted a ceasefire called for by the United Nations. Agreeing to it, he said, was more deadly to him than drinking poison. The guns fell silent on 20 August 1988, with the border where it had been in 1980.

The war killed about half a million people, some say twice as many, and left both countries deep in debt with nothing to show for it. Iraq's debts led Saddam to invade Kuwait two years later. In Iran the war's martyrs are still remembered on murals in every town.
pts: Eight years of war, and no land changed hands
Poison gas killed thousands at Halabja
